title: Latin America’s China Dilemma: Lessons From Peru and Colombia’s Presidential Elections
gist: Despite China's popularity in Latin America hitting an all-time high, the 2025-2026 electoral super-cycle -- including Keiko Fujimori's Peru win -- has produced a rightward, U.S.-aligned, rhetorically China-skeptic wave of leaders, though deep economic ties to Beijing will constrain any real strategic realignment in Peru and Colombia.

themes.theme: Rhetoric vs. reality on Latin America's China pivot

insights.claim: China's overall popularity in Latin America is at an all-time high even as the region's 2025-2026 electoral super-cycle has swung voters toward candidates who position themselves as U.S.-aligned and, at times, China-skeptic.
insights.speaker: Alonso Illueca
insights.so_what: The disconnect between high public approval of China and elite/electoral rhetoric that skews pro-U.S. suggests investor read-throughs on China-Latin America relations should track government rhetoric and elite alignment separately from underlying popular sentiment or economic ties.
insights.quote: While Beijing’s overall popularity in the region is at an all-time high, Latin Americans are voting in candidates who position themselves as U.S.-aligned and, at times, China skeptics.

insights.claim: Peru and Colombia -- where China policy was not initially expected to be a decisive electoral issue -- both elected presidential candidates (including Keiko Fujimori in Peru) expected to distance their governments rhetorically from Beijing and move closer to Washington.
insights.speaker: Alonso Illueca
insights.so_what: Signals a rightward political realignment across two major Latin American economies with potential implications for U.S.-Latin America trade/security cooperation and for Chinese state-linked investment approval processes going forward.
insights.quote: Even Peru and Colombia, where China policy did not initially appear likely to become a decisive electoral fault line, have elected candidates who are expected to distance their governments from Beijing, at least rhetorically, and move closer to Washington.

insights.claim: Despite the rhetorical pivot toward Washington, deep economic ties between Peru/Colombia and China will constrain any significant strategic realignment away from Beijing.
insights.speaker: Alonso Illueca
insights.so_what: Investors should expect continuity in Chinese trade and investment flows into Peru and Colombia (e.g., mining, infrastructure) even under nominally U.S.-aligned governments, since economic dependence will outweigh political rhetoric in practice.
insights.quote: But in both countries, deep economic ties with China will continue to constrain any significant strategic realignment.
